Introduction Financial well-being has become one of the key indicators for assessing individuals’ quality of life, particularly in the face of increasingly complex global financial challenges. The concept goes beyond the amount of wealth a person possesses—it reflects the ability to effectively manage financial resources to meet present and future needs while avoiding financial stress (Chaudhry et al., 2024). Although research on financial well-being is still relatively new, it has attracted growing academic attention due to its crucial role in bridging the relationship between financial literacy, financial behavior, and financial satisfaction. Studies indicate that low financial literacy can lead to poor financial management behavior, which ultimately has a negative impact on individual financial well-being (Obaid et al., 2023). Moreover, the issue of financial well-being has become increasingly prominent amid global changes, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, which has intensified financial pressure for many individuals. In this context, financial literacy serves as a vital tool that enables individuals to make wiser financial decisions related to spending, saving, and investing—thereby strengthening their resilience against economic uncertainty. This makes financial well-being an urgent topic for further exploration across various social and economic contexts. In the post– COVID-19 context, financial pressures among students have intensified alongside the growing shift toward digital transactions and technology-driven financial inclusion. This situation demands a higher level of financial literacy and psychological management skills, enabling individuals to maintain both financial stability and psychological well-being simultaneously. Financial well-being is an important indicator for assessing an individual’s financial stability and is influenced by various factors, including financial literacy, financial behavior, attitudes toward money, financial stress, financial socialization, risk tolerance, and demographic factors such as age, income, and education level. Financial literacy, in particular, plays a key role by providing the knowledge and skills needed to manage finances effectively—such as developing saving habits, budgeting, and avoiding excessive or impulsive spending (Mahdzan et al., 2023; Sangeeta et al., 2022). Moreover, healthy financial behavior has been shown to improve individuals’ ability to achieve greater financial stability and well-being in both the short and long term (Sultana et al., 2024). However, there are inconsistencies in the literature regarding the relationship between financial literacy and financial well-being. Some studies report a significant relationship, while others find that the impact is often mediated by variables such as financial behavior, self-efficacy, or technical skills in managing financial products (Kumar et al., 2023; Manalo et al., 2024). These inconsistencies highlight the need for further research to better understand the underlying mechanisms of this relationship, particularly by considering contextual factors such as social and economic background. Future studies could adopt a multidimensional approach that integrates cognitive, behavioral, and environmental aspects to uncover more complex dynamics, thereby making a meaningful contribution to the growing body of literature on financial well-being. Building on the reviewed literature, this study offers a distinct approach compared to previous research by integrating psychological aspects—such as self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting—into the relationship between financial literacy and financial well-being. Prior studies have primarily focused on the direct effects of financial literacy on financial well-being or on the mediating role of general financial behaviors such as saving or debt management (Mahdzan et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2023). However, this study expands the theoretical framework by emphasizing psychological variables that influence how individuals make financial decisions, manage their resources, and achieve financial well-being. Self- control serves as a regulator of impulsive consumption, enabling individuals to delay gratification for long-term financial goals—an area that has rarely been explored in depth in earlier studies. Additionally, mental budgeting, or the ability to allocate income into specific categories, is considered a key mechanism for effective financial management, particularly for individuals with limited income, such as students. Meanwhile, mental accounting, which involves mentally categorizing income and expenditures, provides a novel perspective for understanding how individuals assign cognitive meaning to their financial decisions (Bai, 2023; Antonides et al., 2011). This study is also unique in its application of the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory as its theoretical foundation. The theory explains how individuals utilize and protect the resources they possess—including cognitive resources such as financial literacy and self-control—to cope with stress and achieve financial well-being (Hobfoll, 1989). COR Theory provides a conceptual framework to explain how psychological variables function as mediators that strengthen the relationship between financial literacy and financial well-being. Through this multidimensional approach, the study not only offers theoretical contributions but also provides practical insights for developing more holistic financial literacy programs that integrate both cognitive and psychological dimensions. This study holds strong urgency based on several key aspects—namely, the phenomenon, the research gap, and its distinction from previous studies. From a phenomenological perspective, university students today face significant financial challenges, such as rising education costs, reliance on limited income sources, and exposure to impulsive consumption driven by the convenience of e-commerce. These conditions place students at a high financial risk if they lack sufficient financial literacy to manage their finances effectively. As the young generation who will serve as future economic agents, it is essential to understand how financial literacy influences students’ financial well-being, particularly through psychological mechanisms such as self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting. Previous studies have largely focused on the direct relationship between financial literacy and financial well-being but have rarely integrated psychological variables that could explain the underlying mechanisms of this relationship. This study addresses that research gap by examining the mediating roles of self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting, which have previously been discussed only separately or not explored comprehensively. Furthermore, this research offers a theoretical contribution by employing the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory as a framework to understand how students utilize cognitive resources—such as financial literacy—to protect their financial assets from economic pressures and achieve financial well-being. The study aims to analyze the effect of financial literacy on students’ financial well-being by investigating the mediating roles of self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting. It also seeks to identify the psychological mechanisms that strengthen the link between financial literacy and financial well-being, providing new insights for policymakers and educational institutions in designing more targeted and effective financial literacy programs for students. Although numerous previous studies have confirmed the role of financial literacy in influencing financial well-being, a significant research gap remains in understanding the psychological mechanisms that mediate this relationship. Most prior research has focused on general financial behaviors as mediators, without exploring the specific roles of psychological resources such as self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting, which shape how individuals manage and give meaning to their financial resources. To address this gap, the present study aims to analyze the effect of financial literacy on students’ financial well-being by incorporating these three psychological dimensions as mediating variables. Theoretically, this study contributes by applying the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory to explain how cognitive and psychological resources are utilized to maintain and enhance financial well-being—a perspective that remains relatively underexplored in the field of personal finance. Practically, this research offers a conceptual framework that can be used by educational institutions and policymakers to design more holistic and psychology-based financial literacy programs, aimed at strengthening the financial resilience and well-being of the younger generation in the digital economy era. The Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory, developed by Hobfoll (1989), provides a strong theoretical foundation for understanding how individuals protect, maintain, and accumulate the resources they possess. This theory emphasizes the importance of various types of resources—physical, social, and cognitive—in helping individuals cope with stress and pressure, including financial stress. In the financial context, financial literacy can be viewed as a vital cognitive resource, as it equips individuals with the ability to understand key financial concepts such as income management, saving, investment, and financial risk. With adequate financial literacy, individuals—including students—are better able to make rational and strategic decisions, allowing them to protect and optimize their financial resources. Halbesleben et al. (2014) describe this process as a “gain spiral,” where the accumulation of resources enhances individuals’ capacity to manage financial pressures, ultimately contributing to improved financial well-being. Conversely, a lack of financial literacy can trigger a “loss spiral,” in which individuals lose control over their resources and become more vulnerable to financial stress. Thus, COR Theory explains that financial literacy not only directly influences financial well-being but also serves as a protective mechanism against the loss of financial resources, helping to reduce financial strain (Hobfoll, 2001; Halbesleben et al., 2014; Hobfoll, 2018). According to the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory (Hobfoll, 1989), individuals strive to acquire, preserve, and protect valuable resources, including cognitive resources such as financial literacy. Financial literacy provides the knowledge and skills that enable individuals to make more rational and strategic financial decisions—such as understanding risks, managing debt, and optimizing investments (Lusardi & Messy, 2023; Chettri et al., 2024). With adequate financial literacy, individuals are able to avoid harmful financial practices, build self-confidence, and reduce financial stress—all of which contribute to improved financial well-being. Moreover, financial literacy enhances financial inclusion and broadens access to formal financial services, which are crucial for strengthening economic resilience in the post-pandemic era. Therefore, the higher an individual’s level of financial literacy, the greater their ability to achieve sustainable financial well-being. Hence, the first hypothesis is proposed as follows: H1: Financial literacy has a positive effect on financial well-being. The concept of mental accounting (Thaler, 1985; 1999) explains how individuals categorize their income and expenses into specific “mental accounts” to simplify financial management. Financial literacy plays a crucial role in shaping a more systematic mental accounting structure, as it provides individuals with knowledge about budgeting, expenditure planning, and consumption control (Rodríguez-Correa et al., 2025). Individuals with higher financial literacy are more likely to consciously establish budget categories, prioritize essential spending, and avoid impulsive or excessive consumption behaviors (Muehlbacher & Kirchler, 2019). In the context of students, this ability is particularly relevant, as it helps them allocate limited financial resources more effectively toward educational needs and future savings. Therefore, good financial literacy is 106 expected to enhance an individual’s ability to apply mental accounting effectively. Hence, the second hypothesis is formulated as follows: H2: Financial literacy has a positive effect on mental accounting. Heath and Soll (1996) describe mental budgeting as a cognitive process in which individuals set spending limits based on specific categories to maintain financial discipline. Financial literacy functions as a cognitive resource that enables individuals to understand the importance of budgeting and expenditure control (Hoque, 2017). With stronger financial knowledge, individuals are able to establish and adhere to spending limits for essential needs, leisure, and savings, thereby preventing wasteful behavior and maintaining long-term financial stability (Antonides et al., 2011). For students, this ability is particularly important as it helps them optimize limited financial resources and guide their financial behavior toward sustainable wellbeing. Hence, the third hypothesis is formulated as follows: H3: Financial literacy has a positive effect on mental budgeting. Self-control is a crucial psychological aspect of individual financial management. According to Baumeister et al. (2002) and Tangney et al. (2004), self-control reflects an individual’s ability to resist short-term consumption impulses in order to achieve long-term financial goals. Financial literacy acts as a cognitive resource that strengthens this ability by providing a deeper understanding of the consequences of financial behavior (Fernández-López et al., 2023; Ogundare et al., 2024). Individuals with higher financial literacy tend to be more disciplined in managing expenses, delaying gratification, and allocating funds toward priority needs. Thus, financial literacy enhances an individual’s capacity for self-control in making sound and sustainable financial decisions. Hence, the fourth hypothesis is formulated as follows: H4: Financial literacy has a positive effect on self-control. The Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory posits that individuals strive to protect and utilize their resources to reduce stress and achieve overall well-being (Hobfoll, 1989, 2001). In this context, mental budgeting, self-control, and mental accounting function as key psychological resources that help individuals maintain financial balance. Mental budgeting provides a cognitive framework for managing expenditures and ensuring efficient use of resources (Antonides et al., 2011). Individuals with strong mental budgeting skills are able to classify and monitor their expenses effectively, which in turn enhances their level of financial well-being (Bai, 2023). Self-control enables individuals to resist impulsive spending and stay focused on long-term financial goals (Khurshid et al., 2021). It is also a major determinant of financial stress, as individuals with higher self-control tend to experience lower levels of financial strain (Raaij et al., 2023). Meanwhile, mental accounting helps individuals prioritize essential expenditures and minimize wasteful spending (Radianto et al., 2024). Psychologically, mental accounting plays an important role in shaping financial decision-making processes, which directly influences an individual’s psychological and financial well-being (Antonides & Ranyard, 2017). Together, these three mechanisms foster more structured financial management, reduce economic stress, and ultimately improve financial well-being. Accordingly, the fifth to seventh hypotheses are as follows: H5: Mental accounting has a positive effect on financial well-being. H6: Mental budgeting has a positive effect on financial well-being. H7: Self-control has a positive effect on financial well-being. Fig. 1. Research Model 2. Methods This study employs a quantitative survey approach to examine the relationships among variables in the proposed research model. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated “strongly disagree” and 7 indicated “strongly agree.” The population consisted of university students from four cities in Indonesia—a group that has received limited attention in previous studies on financial well-being. Using purposive sampling, respondents were selected based on specific criteria: they had to be active students, possess basic knowledge of personal finance, and be willing W. E. D. Radianto et al. / Decision Science Letters 15 (2026) 107 to participate. A total of 800 questionnaires were distributed to ensure an adequate sample size for analysis using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), which is recognized for its strength in modeling complex predictive relationships, even with relatively small sample sizes. The operational definitions of variables were derived from established theories and prior studies: financial literacy (Setiawan et al., 2021) was measured by five indicators; financial well-being (Powell et al., 2023) by five indicators; self-control (Thung et al., 2012) by five indicators; mental budgeting (Antonides et al., 2011) by four indicators; and mental accounting (Radianto et al., 2024) by nine indicators. Data analysis was conducted using SmartPLS, with PLS-SEM chosen for its predictive capability and flexibility in handling non-normally distributed data. The analysis included two main stages: the outer model, which tested validity and reliability using outer loadings, Average Variance Extracted (AVE), Composite Reliability (CR), and discriminant validity through the Fornell-Larcker criterion and Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT); and the inner model, which evaluated relationships among latent variables using path coefficients, t-statistics, and p-values. The model’s predictive power and construct contributions were further assessed through R-square, f-square, and Q-square values. The use of PLS-SEM in this study provides a predictive and flexible framework, making it suitable for exploring the psychological and financial factors that influence students’ financial well-being, thereby offering comprehensive and empirically grounded insights. 3. However, for the Self-Control construct, the Adjusted R-square value of 0.018 is categorized as weak (<0.19), W. E. D. Radianto et al. / Decision Science Letters 15 (2026) 111 indicating that the model has a very limited predictive power for this construct. These findings imply that while the model performs well in predicting key constructs such as Financial Wellbeing, its predictive strength varies across different constructs. As suggested by Hair et al. (2017), a Q²predict value greater than zero signifies that the model has relevant predictive capability. In this model, the Financial Wellbeing construct has a Q²predict value of 0.531, demonstrating a very strong predictive ability for this variable. The constructs Mental Accounting and Mental Budgeting have Q²predict values of 0.515 and 0.513, respectively, also indicating high predictive relevance. However, the Self-Control construct shows a Q²predict value of only 0.015, which is very low, suggesting that the model lacks significant predictive relevance for this construct. Additionally, the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) values provide further insight into prediction errors. Financial Wellbeing recorded an RMSE of 0.686 and an MAE of 0.515, indicating relatively small prediction errors compared to other constructs. For Mental Accounting and Mental Budgeting, the RMSE and MAE values are nearly equivalent, suggesting a similar level of prediction accuracy for both constructs. Conversely, Self-Control exhibits higher prediction errors, with an RMSE of 0.995 and an MAE of 0.831, which aligns with its low Q²predict value. Overall, the model demonstrates strong predictive relevance for the key constructs — Financial Wellbeing, Mental Accounting, and Mental Budgeting — but shows limited predictive capability for the Self-Control construct. Furthermore, the Normed Fit Index (NFI) value of 0.887 suggests that the model is approaching a good level of fit, though it falls slightly below the recommended threshold of 0.90. Overall, the results indicate that the model achieves a moderately good fit, demonstrating acceptable adequacy for further interpretation and analysis. 4. Discussion The findings of this study confirm that financial literacy has a significant influence on financial wellbeing, both directly and through psychological mediating variables such as self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting. Within the framework of the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory (Hobfoll, 1989), financial literacy functions as a cognitive resource that enables individuals to acquire, maintain, and protect their financial assets. Students with higher levels of financial literacy tend to adopt more efficient financial management strategies to cope with limited resources—such as planning expenditures, setting aside emergency savings, and avoiding impulsive spending. Thus, financial literacy serves not only as instrumental knowledge but also as a protective mechanism that enhances financial resilience and reduces economic stress. Furthermore, the study highlights the crucial mediating roles of mental accounting and mental budgeting in linking financial literacy to financial wellbeing. These constructs act as cognitive mechanisms that structure how individuals perceive and allocate their money. From a COR Theory perspective, these processes represent resource conservation strategies, where individuals mentally organize their finances to prevent unnecessary losses. Students with strong financial literacy are more capable of developing a “protective framework” by categorizing expenditures, distinguishing needs from wants, and establishing rational budget limits. Through these mechanisms, they not only improve financial efficiency but also strengthen their sense of control and financial satisfaction. In addition, self-control emerges as the strongest mediator between financial literacy and financial wellbeing. This finding aligns with Baumeister et al. (2002), who posit that self-control is a form of psychological resource that allows individuals to 112 delay gratification in pursuit of long-term goals. In the student context, self-control acts as a behavioral filter that helps balance academic, social, and personal needs. The combination of financial literacy and self-control thus enables individuals to maintain equilibrium between the use and protection of financial resources—reflecting the core principle of COR Theory. From a practical perspective, these results provide valuable guidance for universities and financial institutions. Universities can integrate financial literacy education into compulsory curricula or student welfare programs focusing on financial wellbeing, emphasizing exercises in self-regulation and budget planning rather than merely technical knowledge of financial products. Financial institutions such as banks and fintech companies can collaborate with universities to develop educational financial products that encourage healthy financial behavior—for example, smart saving goals or automated budgeting assistants. Such innovations would strengthen the link between knowledge, behavior, and financial wellbeing among students. Finally, this study contributes to three key dimensions. Theoretically, it extends the application of COR Theory by demonstrating how financial literacy functions as a cognitive resource mediated by psychological mechanisms (self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting) in explaining students’ financial wellbeing. Practically, it offers a conceptual framework for universities, regulators, and financial institutions to design more effective behavioral-based educational interventions aimed at improving the financial wellbeing of young adults. Methodologically, it reinforces the use of PLS- SEM in examining multidimensional relationships between cognitive and psychological variables, providing a foundation for future studies employing longitudinal or experimental designs to test causal pathways. Consequently, this research not only advances theory and practice but also opens new avenues for deepening multidisciplinary understanding of financial wellbeing. 5. Conclusion This study confirms that financial literacy functions not only as technical knowledge but also as a cognitive resource that protects financial wellbeing through psychological mechanisms such as self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting. Grounded in the Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory, the findings indicate that financially literate students are better able to preserve and optimize their financial resources through disciplined self-regulation and planned financial strategies. This process enhances financial security, satisfaction, and resilience against economic stress. The results provide empirical evidence that strengthening financial wellbeing requires a holistic approach combining cognitive (financial knowledge), behavioral (budgeting and self-control), and psychological (perceived security and balance) dimensions. Policy implications suggest that national financial literacy programs should evolve from product-based education toward behavioral-based financial education, focusing on reflective ability and self-regulation in digital financial decision- making. For universities and financial institutions, the findings highlight the need to foster a learning ecosystem that promotes financial mindfulness, disciplined budgeting, and responsible use of financial technology. Theoretically, this study extends COR Theory into the financial literacy context by demonstrating how cognitive and psychological resources interact to shape adaptive financial behavior. Practically, it offers a conceptual model for educators and policymakers to strengthen young adults’ financial wellbeing. Methodologically, the use of PLS-SEM proves effective for explaining multidimensional relationships among cognitive, psychological, and wellbeing variables. Despite these contributions, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design restricts causal inference; longitudinal or experimental studies are needed to capture dynamic changes in financial wellbeing over time. Second, self-report measures may introduce bias; future studies should incorporate behavioral or experience-sampling data to enhance validity. Third, the sample focuses on students from four Indonesian cities, limiting generalization to other populations or cultural contexts. Future research could integrate digital financial behavior and emotional regulation into the model to reflect changes in financial habits due to fintech adoption. Comparative and mixed-method approaches—combining quantitative and qualitative insights—may further deepen understanding of financial wellbeing from a behavioral and cross-cultural perspective. JSON: Name: financial_literacy_psych_mediators Title: Partial least squares structural equation modeling of psychological mediators in the effect of financial literacy on university students' financial well-being Short Hypothesis: Higher financial literacy causes increased financial well-being among university students. Related Work: Existing research has primarily examined the relationship between financial literacy and financial well-being using cross-sectional surveys and structural equation modeling variants; common approaches either estimate a direct effect of financial literacy on well-being or introduce broad behavioral mediators (e.g., saving, debt management) and self-efficacy. Prior methods often rely on covariance-based SEM for theory testing or PLS-SEM for predictive modeling, and some work has examined single psychological constructs such as self-control or mental budgeting in isolation. Limitations across the literature include inconsistent findings on direct effects, limited investigation of specific psychological mediators jointly, reliance on self-reported single-source data, weak attention to discriminant validity among related cognitive constructs, and frequent cross-sectional designs that prevent causal inference. Few studies combine multiple psychological mediators (self-control, mental budgeting, mental accounting) within a single resource-theoretic framework and evaluate both predictive performance and mediation simultaneously. Abstract: This research operationalizes financial literacy as a cognitive resource and evaluates its effect on student financial well-being through three psychological mediators: self-control, mental budgeting, and mental accounting. Using a survey-based design and partial least squares structural equation modeling, the study estimates direct and indirect path coefficients, model predictive power, and construct validity for a multi-mediator model. The main contribution is an integrated, resource-theoretic empirical pipeline that quantifies how specific psychological mechanisms transmit the effects of financial knowledge to subjective financial outcomes and compares nested models to isolate mediator contributions. Expected outcomes include statistically significant direct and mediated effects of financial literacy on well-being, differing effect sizes across mediators, and demonstrable gains in explained variance when psychological mediators are included. The pipeline produces reproducible measurement and structural tests that inform targeted behavioral interventions and provide a benchmark for subsequent causal or longitudinal studies. Experiments: Dataset: cross-sectional survey of N≈800 active university students sampled across four Indonesian cities; instrument contains constructs with the following indicators: financial literacy (5 items), financial well-being (5 items), self-control (5 items), mental budgeting (4 items), mental accounting (9 items). Preprocessing: remove indicators with outer loadings <0.70; handle missing data via listwise deletion if <5% missing, otherwise multiple imputation; standardize items. Primary model: PLS-SEM with reflective measurement models and bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to estimate path coefficients, t-statistics, p-values, and bias-corrected 95% CIs. Evaluation metrics: path coefficients and p-values, R2 and adjusted R2 for endogenous constructs, f2 effect sizes for each predictor, Q2predict and out-of-sample RMSE/MAE, SRMR, d_ULS, d_G, HTMT and Fornell-Larcker for discriminant validity, VIF for collinearity. Baselines: (A) direct-only model (financial literacy → financial well-being), (B) single-mediator models (financial literacy → each mediator → well-being) run separately, (C) full mediation model (all three mediators), (D) CB-SEM (covariance-based SEM with ML estimation) for confirmatory comparison, (E) predictive ML baseline (regularized linear regression and random forest) predicting financial well-being from the same items aggregated. Ablation studies: sequentially remove each mediator from the full model and record ΔR2, change in direct path coefficient, and mediation significance; run multigroup PLS-SEM by gender and city to assess heterogeneity. Robustness checks: bootstrap mediation (5,000), permutation tests for Q2predict, and sensitivity to indicator removal (leave-one-indicator-out). Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal attribution and temporal sequencing of mediator effects. Self-report measures introduce common method variance and social desirability bias. Sample composition (majority female and concentration in specific disciplines/cities) limits external generalizability across populations and cultures. Measurement risk: high collinearity between mental budgeting and mental accounting can inflate variance and bias mediator estimates. The self-control construct may exhibit low explained variance (weak R2) reducing mediation detectability. PLS-SEM model fit indices (SRMR, d_ULS) are sensitive to misspecification and large sample chi-square inflation; alternative methods (CB-SEM) may produce conflicting results. Predictive baselines (random forest) optimize different objectives than SEM, complicating direct comparison. Missing or non-random nonresponse could bias estimates. The pipeline does not by itself address unobserved confounding or endogeneity between literacy and psychological traits.
